name: Ganggangsullae

narrator.name: The Atlas narrator
narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which
narrator.languages: master narration in English; translations per language in episodes/i18n/<lang>/<slug>.json with the same scene structure (pipeline/translate.py); names, places and counts are never translated

instructor.persona: A community elder or traditional dance educator.
instructor.rule: counts out loud; demonstrates front and back; three slow repetitions before tempo; one correction at a time

scenes.title: Cold open
narration: Under the full moon of the Chuseok harvest, women once used this circle dance as a military ruse, dressing in uniform to trick invaders into overestimating the size of the Korean army.
This is Ganggangsullae. Pre-colonial to present.
on_screen: Hero video, first 10 seconds (TlZrnxCxogo)
Title card: Ganggangsullae · South Korea · Pre-colonial to present

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance originated in the southwestern coastal regions of Korea.
It is associated with ancient agricultural rites and the Joseon Dynasty, where it served as a social outlet for women.
Legend credits Admiral Yi Sun-sin with using the dance as a military ruse during the 16th-century Japanese invasions.
on_screen: Map: South Korea · East Asia
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: It is performed during Chuseok, Daeboreum, and other major Korean festivities.
It symbolizes fertility, harvest, communal harmony, and feminine solidarity.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance begins in a circle, moving counterclockwise.
Participants hold hands, with the back of the right hand above and the palm of the left hand above.
Footwork involves walking with the heel touching the ground first, transitioning to faster running where knees are raised.
Watch for Wonmu, Gatekeeper Play.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (TlZrnxCxogo)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Circle, spiral, concentric circles, and lines.
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music relies on 'jangdan' rhythmic patterns.
The primary instruments are the 'janggu' (hourglass drum) and 'buk' (barrel drum).
Listen for the Janggu, Buk.
The pulse is Jangdan rhythmic cycle..
A rhythmic, percussive soundscape driven by the janggu drum, layered with a communal, melodic call-and-response vocal chant that increases in speed and intensity.

Form: Progressive tempo increase.. Mood: contemplative, energetic, communal.
